newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African bond market turnover up 50 pct in 1996.
newsitem.headline: S.African bond market turnover up 50 pct in 1996.

text.p: Turnover on the South African Bond Exchange jumped more than 50 percent in 1996 as speculative interest in the local gilts market soared, statistics released by the exchange on Wednesday show.
The exchange said trades totalling 3,002 billion rand were recorded last year compared with the 2,006 billion rand registered in 1995.

Foreigners accounted for 11 percent of total market volume and were net buyers of 3.384 billion rand's worth of South African bonds in the year. Statistics for the previous year were not provided as the exchange only began compiling these in mid-1995.

The statistics show, however, that in the six months to December 31, 1996, foreigners were net buyers of just 635 million rand's worth of bonds compared with 4.353 billion rand in the same period in 1995.

Foreigners sold South African bonds heavily in the aftermath of the rand's plunge which started in February last year, ditching over 2.5 billion rand worth of bonds in March and April after buying 2.6 billion rand in January and February.
That trend was reversed, however, in most of the remaining months of the year, with the notable exception of August when foreigners were net sellers of 1.3 billion rand worth of stock.
Turnover in the benchmark government stock -- the R150 -- more than doubled in the year to 1,213 billion rand from 568.37 billion rand in 1995.

The yield on the R150 moved from a year-low of 13.33 percent on February 15 to a year-high of 16.57 on May 9 before settling at around 16.10 percent at the end of the year. It is currently trading around 15.92 percent.
The longer-dated R153, which matures in 2010, was the next most traded stock, with 454.82 billion rand worth of trades being registered last year, up from 263.97 billion rand the year before.
Nominal values traded by issuers grew 46.2 percent to 3,405 billion rand from 2,329 billion rand in 1995.
The South African government accounted for the bulk of trades, registering 2,446 billion rand's worth, while Eskom was the next biggest at 341.57 billion rand.
The exchange also began compiling monthly data in mid-1996 showing offshore trades concluded by non-residents which do not fall within its regulatory jurisdiction.
It said that in December 1996, some 3,504 offshore transfers of stock were recorded compared with 4,212 in November and 4,548 in October.
Offshore trade volumes were pegged at 19.437 billion rand in December from 23.81 billion rand in November and 32.42 billion rand in October.
